lines.text: Welcome to JavaScript Demystified: interview edition.
Today, we answer four of the most common JavaScript interview questions.
For each one, you get a short answer you can say out loud, a demo that proves it, and the follow-ups interviewers love.
Let's get started.
Question one. What is the difference between [==|double equals] and [===|triple equals]?
Here is the short answer.
[===|Triple equals] compares the value and the type, with no conversion.
[==|Double equals] converts the types first, and then compares.
That conversion is called type coercion, and it is where the surprises come from.
And when both sides already have the same type, [==|double equals] behaves exactly like [===|triple equals].
Let's test it.
Zero [==|double equals] false is true, because false is converted to zero.
But zero [===|triple equals] false is false, because a number is not a boolean.
The string one [==|double equals] the number one is true. [===|Triple equals] says false.
Null [==|double equals] undefined is true. [===|Triple equals] says false.
[NaN|Not a number] is never equal to anything, not even itself.
To check for it, use [Number.isNaN|Number dot is N A N].
And two empty arrays are not equal either, because they are two different objects.
So in an interview, say this: use [===|triple equals] by default.
A common exception is [== null|double equals null], which checks for null and undefined in one go.
Question two. What is the difference between var and let?
Short answer: var is function scoped, and let is block scoped.
Both are hoisted. But var starts out as undefined, while let stays uninitialized until its declaration line.
That gap is called the temporal dead zone.
Look at this code. What will this print?
The first line prints undefined. The variable a exists, and it holds undefined.
The second line throws a reference error.
The variable b exists too, but it is in the temporal dead zone.
Now scope. Inside this block, var x leaks out to the whole function.
But let y stays inside the block. Outside, it does not exist.
Two more differences.
var lets you declare the same name twice. let throws a syntax error.
And const works like let, but you cannot reassign it.
If it holds an object, the object itself can still change. const protects the variable, not the value.
One last difference, in the browser: a top level var also becomes a property on window. let does not.
In modern code, prefer const, then let, and avoid var.
Question three. What is the difference between call, apply, and bind?
Short answer: all three let you choose what this points to inside a function.
Call and apply run the function immediately. Bind returns a new function to run later.
Call and apply differ in how you pass the arguments.
A handy memory trick: call takes a comma separated list. Apply takes an array.
Here is a function that greets whoever this points to.
With call, we say: run greet, with this set to Ava, and pass the arguments one by one.
With apply, it is the same idea, but the arguments go in an array.
Both run right away.
With bind, nothing runs yet. We get back a new function, with this permanently set to Ava.
Call it later, and this is still Ava.
Bind is what you reach for when you pass a method as a callback, and you don't want to lose this.
Now, three bonus facts that interviewers love.
One. Bind can preset arguments. This is called partial application.
Bind Ava and hi, and later, you only pass the punctuation.
Two. A bound function cannot be rebound. Calling it with Ben still says Ava.
Three. Arrow functions ignore call, apply, and bind for this. They take this from where they were written.
And one modern tip: apply is mostly replaced by the spread operator.
Question four. What is the difference between [Promise.all|promise dot all] and [Promise.race|promise dot race]?
Short answer: all waits for every promise. Race finishes with the first one to settle.
[Promise.all|Promise dot all] gives you an array of results, in the same order you passed the promises in.
But if any promise rejects, all rejects immediately.
Here are two promises. Slow takes half a second. Fast takes a tenth of a second.
[Promise.all|Promise dot all] waits for both. After half a second, we get slow, then fast.
That is the input order, not the finishing order.
[Promise.race|Promise dot race] stops waiting as soon as fast finishes, after a tenth of a second.
Race settles with the first result, whether that is a success or a failure.
Now a popular follow-up. Does [Promise.all|promise dot all] cancel the other promises?
No. Promises cannot be cancelled. The other work keeps running in the background.
To really stop it, use an API that supports cancelling, like fetch with an [AbortController|abort controller].
Two more combinators come up in interviews.
[Promise.allSettled|Promise dot all settled] waits for everything, and never rejects. You get a status for each promise.
[Promise.any|Promise dot any] returns the first promise that succeeds, and ignores the failures.
If every promise fails, any rejects with an aggregate error.
And one trap: [Promise.race|promise dot race] with an empty array never settles.
Let's recap the four answers.
One: [===|triple equals] compares value and type. [==|Double equals] converts types first.
Two: var is function scoped, let is block scoped, and let has a temporal dead zone.
Three: call and apply run now. Bind returns a new function.
Four: all waits for everyone. Race takes the first to finish. Neither cancels anything.
Thanks for watching, and good luck in your interview!
